Toshizō was the one ever-victorious general in the army of the Hakodate government.

The steep ground of Futamata, which this man held with but a single battalion, did not stir a particle for more than ten days, and the government forces that pressed against it were beaten off, every one.
It was, likely, one of the happiest stretches of Toshizō's life.
The soldiers too worked merrily under this brawler.
There were reckless fellows who fired off more than a thousand rounds from a single gun in one day, and the faces of such men went black with the scum of powder-smoke.
The gun-barrels grew so hot the loading-gear would not work. They were burned and blistered by the heat, the skin splitting on their hands.

Toshizō had about a hundred water-buckets carried up from the foot of the hill, and had the men dip their guns in the water and go on firing. A water-cooled gun-fight—surely there was no one who fought such a thing even in the Europe of that day.
"There's ball without end. Fire, fire, fire away,"
he cried, going the round of the positions to hearten them.
The pass where this man's whole force lay entrenched,
"Futamata,"

was one of the range of hills behind Hakodate Bay, ten ri from the town of Hakodate. Along it ran the byway from Esashi on the Japan Sea coast into Hakodate, and the government forces, seeking to strike at Hakodate harbor from behind, must of necessity pass this way.

If one sought its type in strategic geography, it answered to such places as Shōjusan and 203-Meter Hill in the siege of Port Arthur in the Russo-Japanese War: let this fall, and the town of Hakodate would be looked down upon from above, laid bare as if stripped naked. Speaking of the Russo-Japanese War, Enomoto Takeaki would answer to General Stoessel. Quick-witted, and a man of learning. Only, both of them tired of things easily from their youth. (Iba Hachirō, head of the Shingyō-ittō-ryū and a shogunal retainer who had fled Edo to join Enomoto's army, is said to have told his youngest brother Sōtarō, on leaving Edo: "This Enomoto is a man of weak will; he cannot carry this war through to the end." Such an estimate of Enomoto was fairly current at the time.)

As for the Russian land forces at Port Arthur, Hijikata Toshizō closely resembles Major-General Kondratenko. Both were ill-bred. Both were unlettered, yet the fondest of fighting and the most skilled at it, and drew to themselves the whole trust of officers and men. After Major-General Kondratenko's death in battle the spirit of Port Arthur suddenly declined, and he made one of the chief causes of its having to open its gates so early as it did.
Futamata is nowadays commonly called by such names as Nakayama Pass, or Uzuragoe.
The pass road ran between Hakamagoshi-yama (613 meters) to the north and Katsuradake (734 meters) to the south, and in Toshizō's day was so narrow that a single horse could just barely pass.
One may call it a natural fastness.
On this road Toshizō pitched a Western-style headquarters tent, lately bought from a foreign trading house in Hakodate, and had his men, too, pitch their portable tents and bivouac.

Around him there were no Shinsengumi troopers. A few were left, but as they were serving as captains of this corps or that, scattered over the several districts, the Futamata position held only Western-drilled soldiers.
From the main camp at Goryōkaku, Enomoto's dispatch officers came almost daily.
Enomoto seemed unable to keep from worrying over the state of the fighting.
"It's all right,"
was all Toshizō would say.

On perhaps the umpteenth time, Toshizō, rare for him, spoke a large boast: "You only wear out your horses' straw shoes. If the state of the fighting changes, I'll send word myself. Tell them the Satsuma and Chōshū men have taken the realm, but Futamata alone they shall not take."
In the headquarters tent there also lodged the French military instructor, Holtan.
When, in camp, Toshizō was busily setting down haiku in his verse-book, he found it a great curiosity and asked what it was.
"Haikai,"
Toshizō answered bluntly, and an infantry captain named Yoshizawa Daijirō, who had a little French, interpreted.
Shinobirika—see it from where you will, the moon of Ezo.
So it stands in the verse-book.
Shinobirika was the one Ainu word Toshizō had learned since coming to this country. It seems to mean "exceedingly fine."
"Is Your Excellency an artist?"
said this non-commissioned officer of the French army, with a slightly odd look.
"This 'artiste'—what is it?"

asked Toshizō. The infantry captain said, "I think it means a maker of songs, a painter." Though "artiste" carries also the sense of "a master hand," or "a queer sort of person." Toshizō may perhaps have been the queer-sort kind.
For the thing called war, this man had a desire like an artist's.

Enomoto Takeaki, Ōtori Keisuke and the like had, each in his own way, a worldview and a conviction concerning this war. By any reckoning they were politicians rather than men of war. To carry their political thought through, they had raised this war.
But Toshizō was without reward.
As for the artist art itself is the aim, so for Toshizō the brawl itself was the aim, and it was for the brawl that he brawled.
With such a pure motive he had come to this land of Ezo. By any reckoning, among the officers of Enomoto's army he was
"a queer sort of person,"
so he was.
Or perhaps it was in that sense that this French non-commissioned officer had asked whether the master was an artiste.
In the defense of Futamata, Toshizō created this war with almost an artist's rapture.
Blood and swords and powder were the materials of Toshizō's art.
The government's field headquarters begged Tōkyō over and over for reinforcements.

Of the ferocity with which Toshizō and his men fought, those letters used such extreme expressions as "a fierce foe fighting to the death like a cornered rat," or "uncommonly cunning," or "seasoned past belief"; and Kuroda Ryōsuke (Kiyotaka), the staff officer of Satsuma birth, lamented the weakness of his own army,

writing to Tōkyō: "With this government army"—that is, a mixture of the several domains—"a hope of victory is very hard. Only the Satsuma troops and the Chōshū domain are strong. Save for our own domain, the only ones to rely on are the Chōshū men; the troops of the other domains fall several grades below even the rebels. It is the height of sorrow. I beg, if it may be, that after-measures"—reinforcements—"be looked to."
so he wrote and sent to Tōkyō.

But when, on the sixteenth, the government army's reinforcements landed at Matsumae, and further the fleet's coastal bombardment began to tell beyond expectation, the situation was transformed at a stroke.
To Toshizō's Futamata position, reports of defeat from every quarter came thick and fast.

On the seventeenth Matsumae Castle fell; on the twenty-second the Kikonai position held by Ōtori Keisuke (a point seven ri by the coast road from Hakodate Bay) fell; and at this the government fleet began to take up a posture to attack Hakodate harbor directly.
"The spineless fools,"
the artiste of Futamata fumed. Now the only place at the front where the sun-banner still flew was Toshizō's position.
The government forces, having swept the positions of every district clear, gathered a great army at the foot of Futamata, and on the twenty-third of the fourth month at last opened a furious assault.
"So they've come,"
Toshizō, up on the height, narrowed to a thin gleam the thick, double-lidded eyes that in the Kyoto days had been called "like an actor's."

The hard fighting ran on three days and nights. The government forces were beaten off more than ten times, yet came on attacking still. At last, in the small hours of the twenty-fifth, Toshizō chose two hundred men skilled in swordsmanship, formed a drawn-sword corps, and made himself its charge-leader.
To the standard-bearer he gave, not the sun-banner, but the banner of the Shinsengumi, the character "Makoto" dyed white on a ground of scarlet wool.
"A banner of the unlucky quarter for the government forces,"
and taking his place at the head of the two hundred, he sprang out onto the road and, with the rifle-companies covering him, carried through a long-range charge of ten chō.
They clashed.

Toshizō cut and cut. Judging his moment, he had the drawn-sword corps lie down on the cliffs to either side. There the rifle-companies came forward and fired. Then the drawn-sword corps rushed in again.
Repeating this more than ten times, the government forces could bear it no longer and began to break and flee.
At once Toshizō ordered the main body waiting on the height into a general attack, and
"Leave not a single man,"
he charged forward.
The government forces fell for the most part, and Komai Masagorō, an inspector of Chōshū birth, was killed at this time.

But the other fronts were in a state of collapse and general retreat, and Enomoto at the Goryōkaku main camp meant at last to draw in his lines and limit his operations to the defense of the Goryōkaku at Kameda and the town of Hakodate alone.
(Enomoto means to surrender.)
It was at this time that Toshizō's intuition told him so.
For the dispatch officer who came to counsel the abandonment of Futamata had no life in his color.
By that complexion one could sense the air of the main camp.
"Here we are winning,"
and Toshizō would not move.
But from the dispatch officer's lips he heard an astonishing turn in the fighting.

The position at Yafurai, which lay on the road from Futamata to Hakodate, had fallen to the enemy's ship's-gun fire, he said. If the government forces came in, Hijikata's army would be cut off and alone.
There was no help for it: Toshizō came down from the Futamata position he had held, beating off the government forces for more than ten days, and returned to the Goryōkaku at Kameda.
"Hijikata-san, you have done well,"
said Enomoto, meeting the mounted Toshizō at the castle gate, and to the officers and men returning with him too he bowed his eyes, one by one, with tears held in them.
Enomoto had this side to him, and it became a virtue in him that grew into a kind of power of command.
Toshizō, too, did not dislike this side of Enomoto, which Kondō had not had. But in this case the tears were more than were wanted. They told upon the men's spirit.
All of them read in Enomoto's tears a defeat blacker than they had foreseen.
What further astonished him on his return was that several hundred of the shogunal infantry Ōtori had led had deserted.
They were, at root, no samurai anyhow, but townsmen scraped together in Edo and Osaka, and once it came to defeat they had no backbone.
But learning of the fact of that desertion, the infantry in Toshizō's own victorious force were shaken as well, and in the ten days or so after their return a hundred of them vanished.

What dealt a further blow was that the warships that were the very treasure of the Hakodate government's army were lost one after another. The Takao was already gone; the gunboat Chiyodagata ran aground in the offing off Bentenzaki at Hakodate; and the Kaiten, the greatest fighting strength of all, took five shells in a sea-fight within Hakodate harbor, ran up on a shoal, and was made powerless.

The one remaining ship, the Banryū, lost her use through engine failure, and the navy on which Enomoto had most relied was wiped out. This annihilation dealt a great blow to Enomoto and the other officers of naval origin, and their dejection weakened the spirit of the whole army.
The annihilation was on the eleventh of the fifth month, and from this time the whole government fleet came into Hakodate harbor.
At the Goryōkaku main camp, on this day of the navy's annihilation, a council of war was opened in an air of the utmost tension.
"What is to be done?"
that was the question.
But though the field positions had been crushed, besides Goryōkaku the Bentenzaki battery and the Chiyogatai battery at Hakodate harbor were still sound.
"A defense within the walls would be best,"
this was the opinion of Ōtori Keisuke.
But Enomoto and Matsudaira Tarō both urged going out to fight.
Toshizō, as ever, said nothing. There was, by any reckoning, no hope of winning any longer.
"For my part, either will do,"
he said, saying a thing that made no sense. Either way, it was settled that they would lose.
Toshizō had come to think only of his own dying.
In the defensive argument over how the Hakodate government was to survive he had lost all interest.
"That is no opinion at all,"
said Ōtori.
"Then, Ōtori-san, is this a council on how we are to win?"
"Naturally. Is that not what a council of war is? What are you thinking of?"
"I am astonished,"
said Toshizō.
"At what?"
"You mean to win, then?"
Toshizō spoke with a face of deep earnest.
"If it is a council meaning to win, then, things being come to this, it is a waste. But if it is a council merely to make a fight of it, I too have a thought."
"Is not a fight a thing one makes in order to win?"
"Well—carry on, all of you. I'll take the part of listener."

Meanwhile, at the government headquarters, preparations to counsel surrender to the Goryōkaku main camp were already going forward; and before sending a formal envoy of submission, they sought to sound the response within the fortress by putting about, through merchants who passed in and out of Goryōkaku, something no more than a rumor.
When they heard this, Enomoto and the other commanders of Goryōkaku laughed it off, every one; but among the officers and men under them
"Is Enomoto not going to surrender?"
such a doubt spread.
This came even to the ears of Nakajima Saburōsuke, the commander at Chiyogatai, and he came galloping over on horseback.

Nakajima Saburōsuke was a man who had once been a yoriki of the Uraga magistracy, and is known for having gone out in a small boat to parley when Perry arrived on the third day of the sixth month of Kaei 6.
Afterward, by shogunal command, he studied the working of warships at Nagasaki, and later became head instructor at the Naval Training Institute; Enomoto had once been his junior there.
In the last days of the shogunate he was a warship officer of the rank of senior duty-officer of the two guards, but being of sickly body had not taken up active service.

With the collapse of the shogunate he fled to Hakodate under Enomoto together with his eldest son Kōtarō and his second son Eijirō, and had become garrison commander of the Chiyogatai battery, which might be called a subsidiary fort of Goryōkaku. He was forty-nine.

Skilled in poetry and prose and in music, and educated besides in Western learning—a man utterly remote, for all that cultivation, in his look of an old-time warrior, and of a fiercely violent temper.

Later, even after Enomoto surrendered and opened the gates of Goryōkaku, this man alone, with his Chiyogatai battery, did not surrender, and on the fifteenth of the fifth month, under a furious assault of the government forces, after a hard fight he was killed in battle together with his two sons.
"The rumor is surely not the truth?"
he said, coming into the Western-style room of the main camp. As luck would have it, only Toshizō was in the room. Toshizō was, this time too, carefully polishing his boots.
"What is this about?"
said Toshizō, turning round. Nakajima was in Japanese dress, by this man's principle. Before the war opened he had served as Hakodate magistrate.
"Ah—is it Hijikata-dono?"
Seeing him from behind, he had taken him, it seemed, for Enomoto.
"Hijikata, yes,"
"You will do as well. You will have heard. By report, they say Enomoto is to surrender; but it is surely not the truth?"
"I have not heard it. Some idle rumor among the infantry, no doubt."
"That would be well,"
and Nakajima Saburōsuke drew up a chair and sat down, and peering into Toshizō's face, said, "Hijikata-dono."

"It is an ill thing to say, but this Enomoto is a man whose knees give way unexpectedly easily when it comes to the point. In my days at the Naval Training Institute I had him for my junior, so I know him well. If—no, say only if—Enomoto should speak of surrendering, what will you, as army commissioner, do?"
"Well, now,"
Toshizō put on a troubled look. He was, by now, in a frame of mind where others were others and he himself was himself.
"It may sound selfish of me, but whatever Enomoto may do, I have no particular objection. Only, if I am asked what I myself will do, I can answer that."
"What will you do?"
"I had, long ago, a comrade named Kondō. At Itabashi, by ill luck, he died on the blade of the government forces. If I were to live on here—"
Toshizō suddenly fell silent.
He had thought it was not, after all, a matter to be spoken of to another. He began to polish his boots.
Kondō is in the ground.

If he himself were to live on here together with Enomoto and Ōtori and the rest, he would have no face to meet the Kondō in the ground—so Toshizō thought, as he polished his boots, with the ease of a commonplace, of what one might call idle small talk.
